71: Hill explains that emotions—the 'feeling' portion of thoughts—give thoughts vitality, life, and action. Faith, love, and sex mixed together give thought impulses greater action than any singly. Importantly, the subconscious mind translates negative or destructive thought impulses just as readily as positive ones. This accounts for the phenomenon millions experience as 'misfortune' or 'bad luck.' People who BELIEVE themselves 'doomed' to poverty and failure are creators of their own misfortunes through negative BELIEF picked up by the subconscious and translated into physical equivalent. Hill suggests readers can benefit by passing any DESIRE to the subconscious in a state of expectancy or BELIEF that transmutation will occur. BELIEF, or FAITH, is the element determining the subconscious mind's action. He notes nothing hinders one from 'deceiving' the subconscious mind through autosuggestion, just as he deceived his son's subconscious mind. To make this 'deceit' realistic, one should conduct oneself as if ALREADY IN POSSESSION of the material thing being demanded. The subconscious will transmute any order given in a state of BELIEF or FAITH into physical equivalent through the most direct and practical media available.
72: Hill acknowledges that enough has been stated to give a starting point for acquiring the ability to mix FAITH with subconscious orders, noting perfection comes through practice, not merely reading. He draws a parallel: if one can become a criminal through association with crime, one can develop faith by voluntarily suggesting to the subconscious that one has faith. The mind comes to take on the nature of dominating influences. Understanding this truth reveals why one must encourage positive emotions and discourage negative ones. A mind dominated by positive emotions ('positive mental attitude') becomes a favorable abode for faith and can give the subconscious instructions it accepts and acts upon immediately. Under the heading 'Faith Is a State of Mind Which May Be Induced by Autosuggestion,' Hill criticizes religionists for admonishing humanity to 'have faith' without telling people HOW. He asserts this book describes all that is known about developing faith. He then makes a series of powerful declarations: FAITH is the 'eternal elixir' giving life, power, and action to thought; the starting point of all accumulation of riches; the basis of all miracles and mysteries; the only known antidote for FAILURE; the element that mixed with prayer gives direct communication with Infinite Intelligence.
73: Hill continues declaring FAITH as the element transforming ordinary 'vibration of thought' into spiritual equivalent, and the only agency through which the cosmic force of Infinite Intelligence can be harnessed. He states every one of these declarations is capable of proof through autosuggestion. He explains the core mechanism: one comes to BELIEVE whatever one repeats to oneself, whether true or false. Repeat a lie enough and it becomes accepted as truth. Each person is what they are because of DOMINATING THOUGHTS permitted to occupy the mind. Thoughts deliberately placed in the mind, encouraged with sympathy, and mixed with emotions constitute motivating forces directing every movement, act, and deed. Hill then states a significant truth: THOUGHTS MIXED WITH FEELINGS OF EMOTIONS CONSTITUTE A 'MAGNETIC' FORCE WHICH ATTRACTS OTHER SIMILAR OR RELATED THOUGHTS. A magnetized thought is like a seed that germinates and multiplies into countless millions of the same kind. He describes the universe as saturated with radiated energy and 'signals'—from gravity to cosmic rays, X-rays, infrared, visible light, sound waves, radar, radio, and television—though we perceive only the tiniest portion. Thought impulses are likewise 'vibrations' transmitted as electrical and chemical currents among brain cells.
74: Hill acknowledges that while we cannot yet scientifically describe the process, thought impulses appear to be 'out there' somehow, as ESP experiments seem to indicate. Human experience teems with thought vibrations—both destructive (fear, poverty, disease, failure, misery) and constructive (prosperity, health, success, happiness)—just as the atmosphere carries hundreds of orchestrations and voices simultaneously. The mind constantly attracts vibrations harmonizing with whatever DOMINATES it. Any thought, idea, plan, or purpose held in the mind attracts related thoughts, grows, and becomes the dominating MOTIVATING MASTER of the individual. Hill explains how to plant the original seed: any idea, plan, or purpose may be placed in the mind through repetition of thought. This is why readers are asked to write out their Definite Chief Aim, commit it to memory, and repeat it aloud daily until the vibrations reach the subconscious. We are what we are because of thought vibrations picked up through daily environment. Hill urges readers to throw off unfortunate environmental influences and build life to ORDER. Taking inventory of mental assets, one discovers the greatest weakness is lack of self-confidence, which can be surmounted through autosuggestion—positive thought impulses stated in writing, memorized, and repeated until they become working equipment of the subconscious mind.
75: Hill presents his 'Self-Confidence Formula' in five parts. First: I know I have the ability to achieve my Definite Purpose; therefore I DEMAND persistent, continuous action toward its attainment. Second: I realize dominating thoughts will reproduce themselves in outward physical action; therefore I will concentrate 30 minutes daily on thinking of the person I intend to become, creating a clear mental picture. Third: I know through autosuggestion any desire persistently held in mind will seek expression through practical means; therefore I will devote ten minutes daily to developing SELF-CONFIDENCE. Fourth: I have clearly written down my DEFINITE CHIEF AIM and will never stop trying until I develop sufficient self-confidence for its attainment. Fifth: I realize no wealth or position endures unless built on truth and justice; therefore I will engage in no transaction that doesn't benefit all affected. I will succeed by attracting forces I wish to use and cooperation of others. I will eliminate hatred, envy, jealousy, selfishness, and cynicism by developing love for all humanity. I will cause others to believe in me because I believe in them and myself. Sixth: I will sign my name to this formula, commit it to memory, and repeat it aloud once daily with full FAITH that it will gradually influence my THOUGHTS and ACTIONS.
76: Hill states behind this formula is a law of Nature no one has explained, which psychologists named the 'Law of Autosuggestion.' The name matters little—it WORKS for mankind's success if used constructively, but destroys just as readily if used destructively. Those who end in poverty, misery, and distress do so through negative application of autosuggestion. The principle: ALL IMPULSES OF THOUGHT HAVE A TENDENCY TO CLOTHE THEMSELVES IN THEIR PHYSICAL EQUIVALENT. The subconscious mind makes no distinction between constructive and destructive impulses—it works with whatever material we feed it, translating fear-driven thoughts just as readily as courage or faith-driven ones. Hill cites medical history's 'suggestive suicide' cases, telling of Joseph Grant, a bank official who 'borrowed' a large sum without consent, lost it gambling, and when the bank examiner arrived, took a hotel room and was found three days later wailing 'My God, this will kill me! I cannot stand the disgrace.' He soon died—doctors pronounced it 'mental suicide.' Hill compares autosuggestion to electricity: useful constructively, lethal if misused. If the mind is filled with FEAR, DOUBT, and UNBELIEF, the Law of Autosuggestion uses this as a pattern for the subconscious to translate into physical equivalent.
77: Hill declares this as true as 'two and two equals four.' He compares the Law of Autosuggestion to wind that carries one ship East and another West according to how sails are set—it lifts or pulls down according to how one sets the 'sails of THOUGHT.' He includes the full poem 'If You Think You Are Beaten': 'If you think you are beaten, you are... / If you think you dare not, you don't... / If you like to win, but you think you can't, / It is almost certain you won't... / Success begins with a fellow's will— / It's all in the state of mind... / Life's battles don't always go / To the stronger or faster man, / But soon or late the man who wins / Is the man WHO THINKS HE CAN!' Hill notes the emphasized words carry deep meaning. He states that somewhere in one's makeup lies sleeping the seed of achievement which, if aroused, would carry one to heights never hoped for. Just as a master musician draws beautiful music from violin strings, one can arouse the sleeping genius in one's brain to drive upward toward any goal.
78: Hill cites Abraham Lincoln as an example: a failure at everything until well past 40, a 'Mr. Nobody from Nowhere' until a great experience aroused his sleeping genius through the emotions of sorrow and LOVE—coming through Anne Rutledge, the only woman he truly loved. Hill states LOVE is closely akin to FAITH because love nearly translates thought impulses into their spiritual equivalent. His research revealed the influence of a spouse's love behind nearly EVERY person of outstanding accomplishment. For evidence of FAITH's power, Hill directs readers to study those who employed it, heading the list with the Nazarene. Christianity is one of the greatest single forces influencing minds, and its basis is FAITH—regardless of how many perverted its meaning or created dogmas not reflecting its tenets. The achievements of Christ, interpreted as miracles, were nothing more nor less than FAITH. If miracles exist, they are produced only through the state of mind known as FAITH. Hill notes some religionists and self-described Christians neither understand nor practice FAITH. He cites the Old Testament psalmist, the apostle Luke ('Stephen, full of FAITH and power, did great wonders and miracles'), and Mark reporting Jesus: 'Daughter, thy FAITH hath made thee whole.'
79: Hill extends FAITH across religions: the Qur'an states 'Surely those who believe and do good, their Lord will guide them by their FAITH.' Confucius's Analects say 'Hold FAITHFULNESS and sincerity as first principles...This is the way to exalt one's virtue.' The Bhagavad-Gita states 'The FAITH of each is in accordance with one's own nature...A person is known by the faith. One can become whatever one wants to be (if one constantly contemplates on the object of desire with FAITH)' and 'The one who has FAITH, and is sincere, and has mastery over the senses, gains knowledge...one at once attains the supreme peace. But the ignorant, who has no faith and is full of doubt...perishes.' Hill then presents Mahatma Gandhi as the most astounding example of FAITH's possibilities. Gandhi wielded more power than any person of his time yet had no money, no home, no suit of clothes—HE DID HAVE POWER. He created it through understanding the principle of FAITH and transplanting it into the minds of 200 million people. Gandhi accomplished through FAITH what the strongest military power never could: INFLUENCING 200 million minds to COALESCE AND MOVE IN UNISON AS A SINGLE MIND. Hill asks: what other force except FAITH could do as much? He predicts employees and employers will discover FAITH's possibilities, noting the world has witnessed what LACK OF FAITH does to business.
80: Hill states civilization has produced enough intelligent people to learn from Gandhi's example. The world had abundant evidence that widespread FEAR paralyzes industry and business. He predicts leaders will arise from the 'unknown' rank and file—steel plants, coal mines, factories, small towns—applying Gandhi's tactics to business. Business is due for reform: methods based on FORCE and FEAR will be supplanted by FAITH and cooperation. Workers will share profits but must first GIVE MORE to employers and stop bickering by force at the public's expense. They must earn the right to profit-sharing. Most importantly, they will be led by leaders who understand and apply Gandhi's principles, achieving FULL cooperation—power in its highest form. Hill criticizes the current age for taking the soul out of people, driving workers as cold machinery, forced by employees who bargained to get without giving. The future watchword will be HUMAN HAPPINESS AND CONTENTMENT, and when achieved, production will take care of itself better than anything accomplished without faith and individual interest mixed with labor. Because of the need for faith and cooperation, Hill transitions to analyzing an event demonstrating how industrialists accumulate great fortunes by giving before trying to get.
